The depletion of natural resources had a significant impact on the decline of the Wild West era. The rapid expansion of industries such as mining, logging, and agriculture led to the overuse and depletion of resources such as timber, minerals, and fertile land. This depleted resource base led to the decline of many of the region's industries, causing economic decline and instability. 

For example, the mining boom led to the over-extraction of gold, silver, and other minerals, resulting in the exhaustion of many of the richest veins and forcing miners to dig deeper and deeper, resulting in higher costs and diminishing returns. As a result, many mining towns and camps were abandoned, leaving ghost towns in their wake. Similarly, the depletion of timber resources led to the decline of the logging industry, and the overuse of fertile farmland led to the exhaustion of the soil, causing agricultural decline.

Furthermore, the depletion of resources also led to environmental damage and destruction, causing long-term damage to the Wild West region's natural ecosystems. The loss of natural resources and environmental damage disrupted the balance of the region's ecosystems, impacting wildlife populations and the overall health and vitality of the region. 

Overall, the depletion of natural resources contributed significantly to the decline of the Wild West era, as it led to economic decline, environmental damage, and the overall destabilization of the region.
<!-- SOURCE_TURN_001_END -->
